strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper provides both empirical (Fig. 2, MoG and Stokes experiments) and theoretical (Appendix B.3, Theorems B.1/B.2) evidence for the 'Jensen's Gap' that arises when PDE constraints are imposed on the posterior mean E[x0|xt] rather than the final sample, giving a solid conceptual foundation for the proposed method.

The proposed fix (post-hoc distillation with physics loss applied directly to the final student output) is simple, well-justified, and effectively sidesteps the identified theoretical issue rather than just heuristically mitigating it.

Extensive empirical validation across a wide range of PDE benchmarks (Darcy, Poisson, Burgers, Helmholtz, Stokes, Heat, Navier–Stokes, Porous Medium, Stefan) and downstream tasks (forward, inverse, reconstruction), with consistent improvements in both accuracy and PDE-residual satisfaction over strong recent baselines (PIDM, DiffusionPDE, ECI-sampling, D-Flow).

Strong efficiency gains are convincingly demonstrated via compute-matched comparisons (Table 3), showing PIDDM achieves better or comparable quality at a small fraction of the NFEs/wall-clock time of baselines.

Thorough ablation studies (component attribution, distillation backbone choice, diversity preservation via SWD/APDD, teacher-quality and architecture robustness, dynamic weighting, latent-optimization stability) substantially strengthen the empirical case and address plausible reviewer concerns.

Honest treatment of limitations: the paper explicitly notes that its distributional fidelity claims remain empirical rather than proven, and discusses dependency on teacher quality and PDE residual operator reliability.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis (Appendix B.3) is restricted to a toy linear/Gaussian setting with a linear score parameterization; while illustrative, its connection to the nonlinear, high-dimensional PDE settings used in experiments is not formally established, so the explanatory power for real experiments remains largely intuitive/empirical.

Despite explicitly discussing Physics-Informed Distillation (PID, Tee et al. 2024) as closely related work with a similar name, the paper does not include it as an empirical baseline, leaving a gap in the comparison against the most conceptually adjacent prior method.

Fairness of baseline tuning is unclear: several baselines (DiffusionPDE, PIDM) are given the same λ as PIDDM's λtrain rather than being independently tuned, which could understate their best achievable performance and slightly favor the proposed method.

The teacher diffusion model itself is trained without any physics constraint, so the student's constraint satisfaction and distributional fidelity depend heavily on the quality/coverage of the teacher's samples; sensitivity analysis of this dependency (Table 8) is only conducted on a single dataset (Darcy).

Most additional diagnostic ablations (diversity, teacher robustness, dynamic weighting, latent optimization stability) are conducted only on the Darcy dataset, limiting generality of these conclusions to the other seven PDE benchmarks used elsewhere in the paper.

The total computational cost of the pipeline (teacher training + trajectory generation for distillation data + student distillation) is not clearly aggregated against baseline training costs, so the 'lower computation' claim, while true at inference time, could be presented more transparently for the full training pipeline.

strengths: The paper clearly articulates and empirically demonstrates the 'Jensen's Gap' problem (R(E[x0|xt]) vs E[R(x0)|xt]) in existing posterior-mean-based PDE-constrained diffusion methods (PIDM, DiffusionPDE, ECI-sampling), using both a tractable Mixture-of-Gaussians toy setting with analytic scores and a training-time Stokes example.

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning 9+ PDE benchmarks (Darcy, Poisson, Burgers, Helmholtz, Stokes, Heat, Navier-Stokes, Porous Medium, Stefan) and three downstream task types (forward, inverse, reconstruction), with consistent NFE/compute-matched comparisons (Table 3) showing large inference-cost reductions.

A substantial appendix of additional ablations (component attribution, diversity preservation via SWD/APDD, teacher-quality and architecture robustness, dynamic PDE-weight scaling, latent-optimization stability) that address many natural follow-up questions and improve reproducibility.

A toy theoretical analysis (low-rank Gaussian target, Theorem B.1/B.2) gives some principled intuition for why moving physics supervision from score-space guidance to final-sample distillation can reduce constraint-direction error, and the authors are appropriately careful to flag that distributional-fidelity guarantees remain empirical rather than proven in general.
Good reproducibility detail: architecture (FNO), training hyperparameters, dataset generation equations, and baseline implementation details are all specified in the appendix.
weaknesses: The core methodological novelty is limited: the pipeline is essentially vanilla diffusion training + existing flow/consistency distillation techniques (rectified flow, DMD, consistency models) + an added final-sample PDE residual loss during distillation + noise-prompting-style latent optimization at inference (already explored in D-Flow/ECI). The main 'new' idea is applying constraint supervision after distillation rather than during diffusion sampling, which is a reasonable but fairly incremental combination of known components.

Reported baseline performance is suspicious in places: e.g., PIDM has roughly 5x worse MMSE than the unconstrained vanilla Teacher while only marginally improving PDE residual (Table 1, Darcy), which is inconsistent with PIDM's own reported quality-vs-constraint trade-off and raises concerns about whether baselines were adequately tuned/reimplemented, potentially inflating PIDDM's relative advantage.

The theoretical justification (Appendix B.3) is restricted to a linear-score, single-constraint-direction Gaussian toy model; it does not generalize to the nonlinear PDE residuals and nonlinear score networks used in the real experiments, and the paper repeatedly concedes that 'distributional fidelity claims remain empirical,' which is honest but undercuts the strength of the central claim that the method 'removes' the Jensen's Gap rather than merely relocating where approximation error enters.

The student is trained to match the teacher's ODE-integrated x0 via an L2 regression loss; since the teacher itself is trained without PDE constraints, the teacher's own samples may already violate the PDE to a non-trivial degree, and the paper does not clearly analyze how the interplay between data-matching loss and PDE loss resolves this tension beyond empirical ablations (λtrain sweeps), leaving the mechanism somewhat under-explained.

All main experiments use a single architecture (FNO) for both teacher and student; architecture-robustness checks (U-Net, CNN-AE) are confined to a single dataset (Darcy) in the appendix, limiting confidence that results generalize across model classes.

Potential mode-averaging/diversity loss from one-step regression distillation is only lightly probed (SWD/APDD on Darcy and a simple correlated 2D MoG toy case); more complex, genuinely multimodal PDE solution distributions are not evaluated, leaving open whether the one-step student preserves multimodality in harder settings.

The paper's volume of appendix tables (apparently added in response to anticipated reviewer questions) somewhat dilutes a clear, focused narrative, and some reported metrics (e.g., Darcy PDE error for ECI/DiffusionPDE/PIDM all clustering near the unconstrained Teacher's value) raise questions about whether the experimental protocol is fully fair to the compared methods.

strengths: Clearly motivates the central problem (posterior-mean mismatch / Jensen's Gap in PDE-constrained diffusion) with both an intuitive argument and concrete empirical demonstrations (synthetic MoG velocity-field analysis and Stokes training-loss curves) that convincingly show existing posterior-mean-based constraint methods create training/sampling inconsistencies.

The proposed fix is simple and well-motivated: decouple physics enforcement from the noisy diffusion trajectory by distilling a teacher into a one-step student and applying the PDE residual directly on the final sample, which is conceptually appealing and practically effective.

Extensive empirical evaluation across many PDE families (Darcy, Poisson, Burgers, Helmholtz, Stokes, Heat, Navier-Stokes, Porous Medium, Stefan) and across generative, forward, inverse, and reconstruction tasks, with compute-matched comparisons showing favorable accuracy/constraint-satisfaction/compute trade-offs relative to PIDM, DiffusionPDE, ECI-sampling, and D-Flow.

Thorough ablation studies (teacher sampling steps, loss weights, distillation backbone choices, hard-constraint masking, diversity metrics, teacher-quality and architecture sensitivity, dynamic weighting, latent-optimization stability) that substantially strengthen the empirical case and pre-empt many natural reviewer questions.

A toy theoretical analysis (low-rank Gaussian target) offering some formal intuition for why final-sample distillation can reduce constraint violation relative to score-space guidance, together with an honest acknowledgment that the distributional-fidelity claim remains empirical rather than proven in general.
weaknesses: The core methodological novelty is somewhat incremental: it combines known ingredients (deterministic ODE distillation, rectified flow/DMD/consistency-model variants, and PDE-residual loss) rather than introducing a fundamentally new mechanism; much of the technical contribution is in careful empirical tuning and benchmarking rather than new theory or algorithms.

The theoretical justification (Appendix B.3) is restricted to a simplified linear-Gaussian/low-rank model with linear score networks; it is unclear how well this analysis transfers to the nonlinear FNO-based models and complex PDE residuals used in the actual experiments, limiting its explanatory power for the real method.

The student objective in Eq. (5) still combines a reconstruction loss and a PDE loss with a tunable weight λtrain, so the claimed elimination of the quality/constraint trade-off is not fully established — the trade-off may simply move from the diffusion trajectory to the one-step distillation objective, and the paper's own ablations (e.g., Fig. 3b) show PDE error and solution MSE moving in different directions as λinfer varies.

All experiments are conducted on relatively simple, low-resolution (128×128) synthetic PDE benchmarks on regular grids using the same FNO teacher/student architecture family (with only limited UNet/CNN robustness checks); scalability to higher-dimensional, irregular-geometry, or real-world physical datasets is not demonstrated.

Some baselines (e.g., PIDM paired with DPS for downstream tasks) are adapted by the authors rather than using original published implementations for all tasks, which could introduce implementation bias favoring the proposed method; no code release is mentioned, which limits independent reproducibility verification despite the detailed appendix.
